title: Bidirectional Dijkstra in San Francisco: Route Speed ⚡
description: Watch Bidirectional Dijkstra expand two frontiers—one from the start and one from the goal—to meet in the middle and cut search work. This visualization shows exactly how a route-planning engine stays fast at scale.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional Dijkstra: How Modern Route Planners Scale ⚡ — Inside high-scale navigation engines, we meet in the middle. 

In this reel, the algorithm runs Dijkstra from BOTH ends: 
• Forward search from the start node 
• Backward search from the goal node 
• When the best combined path is found, expansions stop early.

Why this matters for shortest path at scale: fewer nodes get relaxed, the priority queues churn less, and latency drops—especially on large road graphs. 

Takeaway: bidirectional search often transforms “explore everything” into “meet efficiently,” which is exactly what production route planning needs. 

Debate question: In your experience, is Bidirectional Dijkstra always worth it, or can graph directionality/weights make it lose?
